item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.6.0: Timelapse + Transcoding UI + ONVIF Enhancements + Documentation Restructure
item.description: Once recording is up and running, storage becomes the first bottleneck. A single 1080p camera writes tens of GB per day — with a 30-day retention policy, a 1TB drive is mostly consumed. Many community members reported the same issue, and during discussions, the ideas of timelapse and transcoding storage gained the most traction: most of the time the scene is static, and compressing it with timelapse requires only 5% of the space for the same duration.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.7.0: Timelapse v2 + Dual-Lens Xiaomi + H.265 Muxing + Release Hardening
item.description: After v0.6.0 put the timelapse pipeline in place, community feedback quickly pointed out several hard problems: the JPEG sequence consumed too much storage, H.265 cameras couldn’t generate playable timelapse segments, dual-lens Xiaomi devices could only capture the main lens, and H.265 HLS would occasionally panic outright. None of these are edge cases — the dual-lens CW500 and Outdoor Cam 4 ship in large volumes in China, and H.265 is the de facto standard for mid-to-high-end cameras. The v0.7.0 mainline was built around exactly this feedback.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.10.0-preview.1: End-to-End H.265 + Timelapse v3 + Auth Modernization + Architecture Cleanup (Paving the Way for Sidecar AI)
item.description:
v0.10.0-preview.1 is MiBeeNvr’s largest release since 0.8.0. The theme isn’t “add features”, it’s clean up the foundation: end-to-end H.265, Timelapse rewritten to v3, low-latency MJPEG, modernized auth, and a sweep of architecture cleanup across config / DI root / API routing / frontend player.

Why this much refactor at this point? After v0.9 paid off the accumulated engineering debt, the NVR’s mainline is heading in two directions — stronger AI capabilities, and support for more cameras. Both require a main process with clear internal structure, pluggable protocols, and AI inference that doesn’t block the video pipeline. The trade-offs discussed in the earlier research posts (frontend codec selection, streaming protocol landscape, NVR remote-access P2P survey, storage media selection) start landing in this release. A dedicated section at the end explains how this cleanup ties into the sidecar AI roadmap.
